stages.title: Chemical thermodynamics
stages.hook: Ice melts above 0 °C but freezes below it, and the heat involved is the same either way. What decides which direction a change goes?
explain: Enthalpy change ΔH is heat exchanged at constant pressure. Hess's law says ΔH for a reaction is the same whichever route is taken, because enthalpy is a state function. So we can add known reaction enthalpies to find an unknown one.

Entropy S measures how many ways energy and matter can be arranged: gases have higher entropy than liquids, and liquids higher than solids. The second law says total entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous change.

Gibbs free energy combines both: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin). A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is negative. If ΔH is positive and ΔS is positive, the reaction becomes spontaneous only at high enough temperature. Spontaneous does not mean fast; kinetics decides speed.

example.q: ΔH = −100 kJ/mol and ΔS = −200 J/K/mol. Find ΔG at 298 K.

analogies.home: A tidy room spontaneously becomes messy; tidying costs effort. Entropy favours mess.
analogies.city: Water runs downhill by itself, like a spontaneous change.
analogies.sport: A ball rolls down a slope on its own but needs a push to go up.
analogies.tech: A phone battery loses charge spontaneously; charging requires input.

stages.mnemonic: G = H − TS: heat and disorder both vote on spontaneity.
terms: A measure of dispersal or disorder of energy and matter.
H − TS; negative ΔG means spontaneous.

misc.wrong: A negative ΔG means the reaction is fast.
misc.right: ΔG says whether a reaction can happen; the rate depends on activation energy.

stages.limits: ΔG predicts spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure; ΔH and ΔS are assumed constant over small temperature ranges.

stages.title: Electrochemistry
stages.hook: A zinc strip in copper sulfate solution slowly becomes coated with copper. Can we capture the electron flow as a useful current?
explain: Redox reactions involve electron transfer. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain (OIL RIG). In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode are separated, and electrons flow through an external wire. A salt bridge completes the circuit with ions.

Standard electrode potentials E° (volts, versus the standard hydrogen electrode) rank the tendency to be reduced. For Zn²⁺/Zn it is −0.76 V and for Cu²⁺/Cu it is +0.34 V. The cell potential is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. A positive E°cell means a spontaneous reaction.

In electrolysis an external supply forces a non-spontaneous reaction. Faraday's law: moles of electrons = Q ÷ F, where Q = I × t and F = 96 500 C/mol. At the cathode Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 2 mol of electrons deposit 1 mol of copper.

example.q: A current of 2.00 A flows for 965 s in a copper(II) sulfate cell. What mass of copper is deposited? (Cu 63.5, F = 96 500 C/mol)

analogies.home: A battery is like a water tank pushing water through a pipe: the voltage is the push.
analogies.city: A water wheel is turned by the flow, as a motor is by electrons.
analogies.farm: A solar-powered fence charger stores electrical energy.
analogies.tech: A phone battery is a cell that is charged by electrolysis in reverse.

terms: Using electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.

misc.right: Electrons flow in the external wire; ions move through the salt bridge.

stages.title: Organic chemistry and functional groups
stages.hook: Methane, ethanol, vinegar and plastic bags all have carbon backbones. How can one element give such variety?
explain: Carbon forms four bonds and can bond to itself in chains and rings, giving millions of compounds. Hydrocarbons contain only C and H. Alkanes are saturated with single bonds and have formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, such as methane CH₄ and propane C₃H₈. Alkenes contain a C=C double bond and have formula CₙH₂ₙ, such as ethene C₂H₄.

A functional group is a group of atoms that decides how a molecule reacts. Alcohols have –OH (ethanol C₂H₅OH), carboxylic acids have –COOH (ethanoic acid), esters have –COO– and amines have –NH₂. Isomers share a molecular formula but have different structures: butane and 2-methylpropane are both C₄H₁₀.

Alkenes undergo addition reactions: ethene + bromine → 1,2-dibromoethane, which also decolourises bromine water as a test. Alkanes burn: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids.

example.q: Give the molecular formula of an alkane with 8 carbon atoms.

analogies.home: Lego with the same bricks in different shapes: isomers.
analogies.farm: Ethanol from fermented crops is used as fuel.
analogies.sport: The same players can form different formations, like isomers.

misc.right: Different arrangements give different properties, such as boiling points.

stages.title: Analytical chemistry
stages.hook: A river sample is tested for dissolved iron. How could you find out how much is there without guessing?
explain: Analytical chemistry finds what is in a sample (qualitative) and how much (quantitative). Titration is a precise method: a solution of known concentration is added from a burette to a measured volume of another until an indicator shows the end point. At neutralisation the moles of acid and base are in the ratio given by the equation.

For HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O the ratio is 1 : 1, so moles = concentration × volume (in litres) for each, and they are equal at the end point. Always do rough and then accurate runs, and average concordant results (within 0.10 mL).

Colorimetry uses the Beer–Lambert law: absorbance A = ε × c × l, where ε is the molar absorptivity, c concentration and l path length. A calibration curve of absorbance against concentration for standard solutions lets us read the concentration of an unknown. pH is −log₁₀[H⁺].

example.q: 25.0 mL of NaOH needs 20.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L HCl. Find the concentration of NaOH.

analogies.home: Adding drops of lemon juice to milk until it curdles: the endpoint.
analogies.farm: Soil testing: sampling a few spots represents a field.
analogies.sea: Measuring the salt in seawater from a small sample.

stages.title: Spectroscopy and chromatography
stages.hook: A forensic lab can tell which dye is in a pen ink from a tiny smear. What tools can separate and identify mixtures?
explain: Chromatography separates a mixture because its components spread between a stationary phase and a mobile phase to different extents. In paper or thin-layer chromatography, the retention factor is Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front, always between 0 and 1. Rf values can identify substances under the same conditions.

Spectroscopy studies how matter interacts with radiation. Energy and frequency are linked by E = hν and c = λν. Infrared (IR) spectroscopy detects bond vibrations: O–H in alcohols gives a broad band near 3300 cm⁻¹ and C=O gives a strong band near 1700 cm⁻¹. UV-visible spectroscopy detects electron transitions, which explains colour.

Mass spectrometry measures mass-to-charge ratios of ions. The molecular ion peak (M⁺) gives the relative molecular mass, and fragments help work out structure. Techniques are often combined, such as gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC-MS).

example.q: A spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent front moves 6.0 cm. Find Rf.
steps: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent.

stages.title: Crystallography and crystal structures
stages.hook: Both diamond and graphite are pure carbon, yet one is the hardest natural material and the other is soft enough for a pencil. What differs?
explain: A crystal has atoms arranged in a repeating three-dimensional pattern. The smallest repeating block is the unit cell. Common metal structures are simple cubic (1 atom per cell, coordination number 6), body-centred cubic BCC (2 atoms, coordination 8) and face-centred cubic FCC (4 atoms, coordination 12). The atomic packing factor is 0.52 for simple cubic, 0.68 for BCC and 0.74 for FCC.

Density follows from the cell: ρ = (n × M) ÷ (N_A × a³), with n atoms per cell, M molar mass, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ and a the cell edge. For FCC copper with a = 0.361 nm, M = 63.5 g/mol and n = 4, ρ ≈ 8.97 g/cm³.

X-ray diffraction finds structures using Bragg's law nλ = 2d sinθ, where d is the spacing between planes. Allotropes, like diamond (a tetrahedral covalent network) and graphite (layers weakly bonded), show how structure controls properties.

example.q: X-rays of wavelength 0.154 nm give a first-order (n = 1) peak for planes with d = 0.154 nm. Find θ.

stages.title: Mechanical behaviour of materials
stages.hook: A paper clip bent once is easy to straighten but after a few bends it snaps. What happens inside the metal?
explain: A tensile test pulls a sample and plots engineering stress σ = F ÷ A₀ against strain ε = ΔL ÷ L₀. At low stress the behaviour is elastic: σ = Eε (Hooke's law), and the sample returns to shape. The slope is Young's modulus: steel is about 200 GPa and aluminium about 70 GPa.

Beyond the yield strength, plastic deformation starts and is permanent; atoms move by dislocation slip. Work hardening makes the metal stronger but less ductile. The maximum on the curve is the tensile strength. Ductility is measured by percentage elongation at fracture, and toughness is the energy absorbed before fracture (the area under the curve).

Under repeated loading below the yield strength, cracks can grow and cause fatigue failure, as in the bent paper clip. Engineers use a safety factor, the ratio of the strength to the working stress, to allow for uncertainty. Hardness resists indentation; creep is slow deformation at high temperature under constant load.

example.q: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa) carries 100 MPa. What is its strain?

stages.title: Phase diagrams and phase transformations
stages.hook: Solder melts over a range of temperatures, while pure lead melts at a single temperature. How can a map tell us what phases exist for any mix and temperature?
explain: A phase is a region of uniform structure and composition. A phase diagram maps which phases are stable at given temperature, pressure and composition. In a single-component diagram like water's, lines separate solid, liquid and gas; the triple point (0.01 °C, about 611 Pa for water) is where all three coexist, and the critical point ends the liquid-gas line.

In a binary alloy diagram, the liquidus is the temperature above which everything is liquid and the solidus is the temperature below which everything is solid. In between, liquid and solid coexist. A eutectic is the composition with the lowest melting point, where liquid turns directly into two solids. The lever rule gives phase fractions: in a two-phase region, the fraction of one phase equals the distance from the overall composition to the other phase's boundary divided by the whole tie-line length.

Gibbs phase rule: F = C − P + 2, where F is degrees of freedom, C components and P phases (at fixed pressure, F = C − P + 1). At the triple point of water, C = 1 and P = 3, so F = 0. Transformations like precipitation need time, so rapid cooling can trap non-equilibrium structures.

example.q: An alloy of 30 wt% B lies in a two-phase region with α at 10 wt% B and liquid at 50 wt% B. What fraction is liquid?

stages.title: Corrosion and materials degradation
stages.hook: Iron ships rust in seawater, yet a zinc block bolted to the hull protects them. How can sacrificing one metal save another?
explain: Corrosion is the electrochemical degradation of a metal. For iron, the anode reaction is Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ and the cathode reaction in neutral water is O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ combine and are further oxidised to hydrated iron(III) oxide, rust. Both oxygen and water are needed, and salt speeds it up by raising conductivity.

Rust flakes off and exposes fresh metal, but some metals such as aluminium and stainless steel form a thin, tight oxide film that protects them: passivation. Galvanic corrosion occurs when two different metals touch in an electrolyte: the more active metal (lower E°) corrodes. Sacrificial protection uses zinc or magnesium, which corrode in place of iron.

Prevention includes painting or coating, galvanising (a zinc coating), alloying (stainless steel with chromium), cathodic protection and control of the environment. Other degradation includes oxidation at high temperature, stress-corrosion cracking and UV damage to polymers. Faraday's law links current to mass loss: m = I t M ÷ (n F).

example.q: A corrosion current of 0.50 A flows for 3860 s, oxidising iron to Fe²⁺. What mass of iron dissolves? (Fe 56, F = 96 500 C/mol)
steps: Moles e⁻ = 1930 ÷ 96 500 = 0.0200 mol; Fe → Fe²⁺ uses 2 e⁻.

teach.topic: Why metals corrode and how to protect them
teach.model: Corrosion is an electrochemical process: the metal is oxidised at the anode while oxygen is reduced at the cathode. Water and oxygen are needed, and salt speeds it. Coatings, alloys and sacrificial metals like zinc protect iron.
